statement: Writes made with an API token record the token as author (stmt owner type `token`, id = token id); the token record names its user.
Replaceable resources return an ETag. PUT, PATCH and DELETE on them accept If-Match and answer 412 when the resource changed, so an agent never overwrites a change it has not seen.

Every JSON error is an RFC 9457 problem (application/problem+json) with type, title, status, detail and instance. `detail` stays the human-readable English message; validation errors add an `errors` list naming each field.

A channel keeps a change feed: every write through an operation, by a person or an API token, and every render status change is one event naming the operation, the item, the actor and the time, never what was written. GET /channels/{slug}/events?since= and MCP list_events list them oldest first from a cursor; waiver events need waivers:read; events are kept SREDITOR_EVENTS_RETENTION_DAYS (30), and an older cursor answers 410.

Every write made with an API token first asks the stmt gate in the channel's scope (operations such as editorial.write); BLOCK or INDETERMINATE refuses it with 403, and a successful write emits its AFTER event, so stmt rules decide and record what agents may do.

Every POST that creates something accepts an Idempotency-Key header, except token creation: its secret is shown once and never stored, so a lost response means revoking that token and creating another. A repeat with the same key and body returns the stored response with Idempotent-Replayed: true; the same key with a different body is refused with 422, and a key whose first request is still running with 409. Keys expire after 24 hours.
An MCP server at /mcp exposes the main operations as tools. Tools call the service layer, never HTTP routes or SQL, authenticate with the same API tokens and enforce the same roles and scopes.

Every MCP tool has a human title and declares all four annotations explicitly: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint (false, since tools act only inside sreditor, except list_voices and generate_voice_over, which call ElevenLabs). An undeclared hint defaults to the worst case, so a tool that only creates or edits would otherwise reach clients as destructive.

The MCP instructions name only tools and operations the server serves, which a test checks, and every caller sees the same tool list. A call whose token lacks a scope or role returns a tool error naming what is missing and how to get it: a new token or connection with that scope, or a role from a channel owner, so an agent can tell an old deployment from a missing permission.

An MCP tool that fails returns a tool error (isError) the agent can act on: what went wrong, the field or value at fault and the call that fixes it, such as the tool that lists valid ids. Protocol errors are only for malformed requests.

MCP moves files through short-lived signed links, since an agent's code cannot use the connection's token: get_file_link gives a single-use https URL, valid 15 minutes, for a brand file, media file, third-party copy, srstudio export, export or book; create_upload_link gives one for an upload into an episode's media, a third-party copy or a brand file slot, checked like the API upload. Files up to 1 MB may come inline as base64. Links never open waivers and need the role and scope of the call they stand for.

Every MCP tool that creates something, uploads or spends credits takes an optional idempotency_key with the API's rules (agentic.idempotency): a repeat with the same key and arguments returns the first result marked replayed, different arguments are refused and keys expire after 24 hours, so an agent can retry after a timeout or a 502 without writing twice.

MCP tools and operations keep no old names: sreditor's MCP has no outside audience yet, so a rename changes the tool, the instructions, every message that names it and the tests together, with no alias or phase-out.
MCP tools return structured content that matches a declared output schema, and list tools page with the same limit and cursor as the API (agentic.pagination), so no result floods the agent's context.

Follow the current MCP specification (2026-07-28): /mcp is stateless Streamable HTTP with JSON responses and keeps no session between requests, so any instance can answer any call. New code adopts none of the deprecated features: Roots, Sampling, Logging, the HTTP+SSE transport and, for clients that can use CIMD, dynamic client registration.

MCP tool names, descriptions and schemas are fixed in code and never built from stored data, so text that people write, such as research notes, sources or screenplays, can never change what an agent is told a tool does.

Group MCP operations by task into a small set of tools: reads apart from writes, ElevenLabs apart, so a client can approve reads alone. A tool takes `request` with the operation's name and its arguments and answers under `result`; its hints are the worst of its operations'. An operation keeps one name everywhere (messages, readiness, search hits). A tool's description says when to use it, when not to and what must exist first, and lists its operations.

MCP clients such as claude.ai connect with OAuth 2.1 as the MCP authorization spec describes: the 401 from /mcp points to protected-resource metadata, and the app is its own authorization server with dynamic client registration, authorization code with PKCE (S256) and a consent page where the signed-in person picks the scopes. Approving issues an ordinary sre_ API token named after the client, so roles, scopes, expiry, revocation, the gate, audit and rate limits apply unchanged.

The authorization server accepts Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and advertises client_id_metadata_document_supported and authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported. It fetches an https client_id URL with SSRF protection (public addresses only; size and time limits), checks the client_id matches the URL and lists the redirect URI, and caches it as HTTP allows. A document listing none among its supported auth methods is a public PKCE client, like ChatGPT's. Registration stays for older clients.

The OAuth endpoints (/.well-known metadata, /oauth/register, /oauth/token) follow the OAuth RFCs, not the API conventions: errors are {error, error_description} (RFC 6749) and registration takes no Idempotency-Key. Redirect URIs must be https or loopback http and match exactly, but a loopback one may use any port (RFC 8252 7.3), as native clients like Claude Code need. Codes are single-use, expire in 10 minutes and are stored only as hashes.
Every API operation has a stable snake_case operationId, a summary and a description written for an agent choosing which call to make.
List endpoints are paginated: `limit` (default 50, at most 200) and an opaque `cursor`; responses are {items, next_cursor}.

Each API token may make at most SREDITOR_AGENT_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE requests a minute (default 120), counted together across the API and /mcp; signed-in sessions are not counted. Every 429 response carries a Retry-After header: the whole seconds until a request is allowed again.

Agents render through MCP: request_render queues a job and answers at once with its id, status and place in the queue, or a tool error listing what the episode still lacks; get_render reports status, progress and report findings and, when done, the video's media file and download link. A video never travels in a tool result: the agent downloads it through the API with the same token, or a person opens the link signed in.

Requesting or canceling a render needs the owner or editor role and, for a token, the render:write scope, and first asks the stmt gate for render.request, so stmt rules can cap how much a channel renders; reading a render needs channels:read. Worker tokens are not user tokens: they can only claim, report and upload jobs.

Agents authenticate with personal API tokens: prefixed `sre_`, stored only as hashes, expiring (default 90 days, at most 365), revocable, limited to explicit scopes and, optionally, to some of the user's channels; other channels answer 404 and a limited token cannot create one. A token never grants more than its user's role, and only a signed-in session can create, list or revoke tokens.
Run subagents on Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5).
Build HTTP APIs with FastAPI.
Write comments that explain why, not what; give every public module, class and function a one-line docstring.
Never hard-code paths, URLs or secrets: read them from settings ([tool.sreditor] in pyproject.toml or environment variables via Pydantic settings).

Change the database schema only through numbered migrations (migrations.py), each run once in a transaction that also records it in schema_version, so a failure leaves the version unchanged. A database without a version is adopted by migration 1, never rebuilt. SQLite stays; the app refuses a database newer than its code.

Keep the relational schema in Boyce-Codd normal form: a column never repeats what another table already holds, unless a constraint keeps both in step. A row that links two items of a channel names the channel in each foreign key, so the database refuses a link across channels; JSON columns hold only a part stored and revised on its own (project.episodes).
Commit no dead code: no commented-out code, unused imports or unreachable branches.
Never use a bare except or swallow an exception silently: catch specific exceptions and either handle them or re-raise with context.
Give a function at most 5 parameters; group related parameters into a Pydantic model.
Keep functions short and single-purpose: cyclomatic complexity at most 10 and about 40 lines at most.
Prefer frozen Pydantic models and pure functions; keep side effects such as database and filesystem access at the edges.
Write all code and schemas in English, including identifiers, comments, and table, column and field names.
Keep layers separate: API routes hold no SQL or business logic and call the store/repository layer, which never imports FastAPI.
Use no magic numbers or strings: name them as module constants or enums.
Define data models and schemas with Pydantic models.
Name things for what they are or do: no abbreviations or single-letter names outside comprehensions, and booleans read as predicates (is_, has_).
Format and lint all Python with Ruff; CI fails on any ruff format or ruff check violation.
Keep test coverage above 90%.

Make each test check one behaviour and name it after that behaviour: test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected>. Exception: a flow test follows one user journey across several pages (registration, password reset, invitation, sign in and out, and the e2e tests) and may check each step in order; name it after the journey and its outcome.
Type-annotate every function signature; the code must pass a strict type check (mypy --strict).

The development deployment is published at https://sreditor-dev.arc4d3.com through the Cloudflare tunnel sreditor-development (zone arc4d3.com); SREDITOR_PUBLIC_URL must match it, and `sreditor doctor` checks that it answers. Production subdomains stay one level deep (name.arc4d3.com), because the free certificate covers only *.arc4d3.com.
Deploy on Docker: ship every service as a Docker image.

Observe the app with Prometheus, Loki and Grafana in compose.yaml under the observability profile: the app serves request metrics labelled by route template on SREDITOR_METRICS_PORT, a port the tunnel never routes to; Grafana Alloy ships container logs to Loki; Grafana provisions both sources and the dashboards in deploy/observability, and only Grafana publishes a port, on loopback, behind a login.

Git keeps the project's rules (stmt scope /) as store/rules.csv, which sreditor render writes from the local store (store/rules.sqlite, never committed) and sreditor rules load reads back. The app keeps its own store in the data volume, with channel guidelines and events, and loads the CSV into it at start; a rule missing from the CSV is disabled, never deleted. Channel data never goes into git.
Generate every document from the stmt store, the single source of truth. Never edit a generated document by hand: revise the statement and regenerate.
Keep the JSON API's error details and field names in English; only text meant for people (pages and emails) is translated.

Mark every user-facing string for translation (_() in templates, N_() in Python) and keep its pt-BR entry in src/sreditor/locales/pt-BR.json; tests fail when a marked string has no translation or a translation has no marked string.
Write every user-facing text in English, the base language, and translate it into Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), the alternate language; English is the fallback for any missing translation.
Choose the language from the ?lang= switch, remembered in a cookie, then the Accept-Language header, then English; set <html lang> to it and send emails in the same language.
Translate stmt prose shown to users, such as terms and privacy, in a sibling category suffixed with the lowercase locale (terms.pt-br); pages fall back to the English category when it is empty.
Draft: this privacy policy has not been written or reviewed yet. Replace this statement with the reviewed text before opening registration to the public.
Rascunho: esta política de privacidade ainda não foi escrita nem revisada. Substitua esta declaração pelo texto revisado antes de abrir o cadastro ao público.

A social account (its platform and handle, ignoring a leading @ and letter case) belongs to at most one channel. A second channel claiming it is refused with 409 and told only that another channel holds it, never which, since channels stay private to their members.

A channel's brand kit holds its identity as data: a display name people can change (the slug stays), colors as #RRGGBB with a role (primary, secondary, accent, text, background), fonts by role (heading, body, caption) with family, weight and an optional font file, logo, avatar and opening and closing stings. Owners and editors change it on pages, through the API (files by PUT and DELETE on a slot) and through MCP (files by upload link); a platform account may override any of it.

An episode lists its claims: each figure or fact its screenplay or short script states, with the quote, where it appears and the sources, its own or its pitches', that back it, each marked primary or secondary and checked or not, with who checked and when. While a claim has no checked primary source the episode warns, without blocking any status, and the warning shows again when it moves to published.

An episode keeps its editorial classification as a part of its own, in the closed vocabulary of Pedro's video-classification 1.0.0 taxonomy: audience, domains, purposes, genres, approaches, formats, visual techniques and styles, tones, emotional targets, creative and humor devices. Each dimension is present, absent, unknown or not applicable; a present one holds one primary and up to two secondary values. Values from an AI or mixed classification carry a confidence from 0 to 1.

A classification whose genres include comedy names at least one humor device; a satirical approach names its target and the behaviour it criticises; a parodic approach names the work it parodies. An agent may propose a classification, but it stays a proposal, marked with its method, until a person reviews it.

A channel declares its profile in the same dimensions, and sreditor observes one from its classified episodes: for each value, how many episodes hold it as primary or secondary and its share of all classified episodes, unknown included. The profile page shows both side by side and warns when a declared primary value appears in fewer than half of the classified episodes.

Episodes, pitches and their sources, media files, third-party media and library entries each keep a context: short answers to what, who, where, when, why and how, stored and revised on its own. Any of them may link to another item of its channel under one of those questions, with a note, such as a pitch whose who is a character; each item lists its links and where it is mentioned. Removing an item removes its context and links. A person outside the library stays a name in the answer.

An episode keeps its delivery package, stored and revised on its own: per cut (such as main, vertical, teaser) the final video (a media file of the episode, or a master registered by reference, never opened) and cover, caption, alt text and hashtags; per platform account and cut (versions A and B share an account) the post link, publish time and optionally its own caption, alt text and hashtags, else its cut's. A post's own text is refused over 5 hashtags or without an AI notice. Publishing only warns.

Reading a delivery package warns, without blocking, when a cut's video runs over SREDITOR_DELIVERY_MAX_SECONDS (default 24), it has more than SREDITOR_DELIVERY_MAX_HASHTAGS hashtags (default 5) or its caption has no line matching SREDITOR_DELIVERY_AI_NOTICE_PATTERN (default: IA or AI as a word, or the words in Portuguese or English; empty turns it off).

A guideline may cite the stmt statement it copies, recording the revision the copy follows; a channel keeps its own copy and may differ. When the statement's text differs from the copy, or it is gone or unreadable, the editorial page, the API read and get_editorial warn with both revisions and texts and never break or overwrite; a person may take the statement's text, an ordinary revision.

An episode belongs to one channel, is numbered within it and moves through the statuses idea, research, script, production and published. Its parts (editorial research, sources and waivers, screenplay, characters, locations, voice-over, sound, visual) are added one step at a time and each is stored and revised on its own, so editing one part never conflicts with another; characters, locations and visual style live in a channel library that episodes refer to.

An A/B experiment links two episodes of a channel, A the control and B the variant, with the change between them, hypothesis, metric, snapshot age, optional platform, status (planned, running, read, abandoned), start day and, once read, the person's reading and verdict; stored and revised on its own. Its result is computed, never stored, from the hand-entered numbers with what_worked's snapshot choice. An episode an experiment compares cannot be deleted until the experiment goes.

Members download ready-made books of a pitch, an episode, the library, the channel or its rights and credits, picking sections, episodes by status or number range, and language: JSON (English field names, format version), Excel (one sheet per table) or a PDF with the channel's logo, colors and library pictures. Exports only read and never include waivers; only the srstudio zip carries audio. Excel cells are always text, never formulas; PDF rendering reads only the app's fonts and the channel's own files.

A channel's library holds third-party media made by others: videos, images, audio, documents, web pages, 3D models, textures and shaders, such as a NASA animation, a YouTube video it reacts to, a credited photo, a paper or a CC BY model. Each item keeps its link, creator, rights (public domain, open license, licensed, citation or fair use, own, unknown) with license and credit line, and may keep an uploaded copy under the episode media file rules. sreditor never downloads from the link.

A 3D model's copy is GLB, binary FBX or BLEND; a texture's PNG, JPEG, WebP, EXR, KTX2 or DDS; a shader's UTF-8 text without control bytes; any of the three may be a ZIP package, stored unopened and always downloaded. GLB and FBX copies show in a 3D viewer built on three.js vendored in static/vendor and loaded only on pages that show one; other files download. An episode may use such an item as a production element.

An episode records each use of a third-party item on its own: the time range or pages, the purpose and the scene. An item in use cannot be removed until its episodes drop it. The episode lists the credits of what it uses and warns, without blocking any status, when rights are unknown, a citation or fair use gives no reason, or a required credit is missing.

An episode refers to its channel library by name: a character who speaks in its screenplay, or a place a scene heading names, matches the library entry with the same name ignoring case and spacing. A name with no entry is offered for adding and never added on its own, so typos do not fill the library.

An episode's media are files: voice-over, sound effects and score as audio (MP3, WAV or M4A), visual effects, final videos (masters made outside sreditor) and renders as video (MP4 or WebM), covers and stills (frames kept as evidence) as images (PNG, JPEG or WebP), each at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES (default 95 MB) except a render (project.render.upload). A video's duration, size and loudness are measured on arrival. The type comes from the content. Each file shows its SHA-256 and has a name and a note.
Media files go to disk in chunks, never whole into memory. A media file never changes, so a new take is a new file; people can change only its name and note.

A published post keeps dated snapshots of its numbers, entered on a page, the API or MCP and not fetched from platforms yet: views, reach, likes, comments, shares, saves, average watch time and retention per second, which may be imported from a platform's CSV. A channel compares its posts by these numbers, so pitches and hooks follow what worked on it.

what_worked groups a channel's published posts by a reviewed classification's primary value, the hook's reaction or length band, or the video's length band, giving per group the posts and the median and mean of one hand-entered number from each post's latest snapshot or the one nearest 1 to 30 days after publishing. Filters: platform, publish dates. Proposals and posts without a value or numbers are counted apart; groups under 3 posts are flagged too small. Hooks have no closed type, so reaction stands in.

A channel keeps pitches (pautas): story ideas with a title, a summary and a status (idea, research, approved, discarded), each with its own research notes and sources, stored and revised on their own. An episode may reference several pitches in order, the first its main one, and a pitch may feed several episodes; an episode shows each pitch's notes, sources and claims as they are, never a copy, next to its own research. A pitch that episodes reference cannot be deleted until they drop it.

sreditor is a social media channel manager and production tool: it manages channels, their accounts on each social platform, their brand kits and their Editorial guidelines, and produces their episodes, from research and screenplay to voice-over, sound and visuals. Build features in service of that purpose.

An episode reads in one call: get_episode_overview and the API's overview give each part's digest with its revision (counts and excerpts, never whole texts) and a readiness list. Each gap has a code, severity, area and fix_tool, a registered MCP tool. In production an srstudio export gap blocks export and render; before production and once published it only warns, and a missing or non-approving latest review warns. list_episodes with readiness and the API count gaps per episode.

Owners and editors can render an episode into video. sreditor queues a job built from the episode's srstudio export at its current revisions and a preset; a render worker builds the scene with srstudio and encodes it with scene-render. The same export, preset, engine version and srstudio commit reuses the earlier video and spends no GPU time. The finished video becomes a media file of the episode (kind render) with its scene-render report.

A worker validates the built scene before any GPU time; one that does not validate fails for good, listing each error. Builds, validations and encodes run under SREDITOR_WORKER_COMMAND_SECONDS (default 6 hours); a tool past it is killed and its job returns to the queue, unless it was the build. Engine output is read only in its formats (scene-render-cli/1 at schema 1.x, scene-render-report/1); output that cannot be read fails the render.

A render job moves through queued, building, rendering, encoding and then done, failed or canceled, and keeps its progress, its worker and the findings of its scene-render report, each with its code, severity, the element and time it concerns and what was measured against which limit. A worker holds a job on a lease it renews while it works; a job whose lease lapses returns to the queue, and one that fails three times stays failed with the reason. A queued or running job can be canceled.

The worker image names scene-render by version and digest and srstudio by commit, never by a tag or branch alone, since either can move. The instance pins the same version (SREDITOR_RENDER_ENGINE_VERSION) and commit (SREDITOR_RENDER_BUILDER_VERSION) and refuses a worker that reports others.

A render in which scene-render passed something through instead of drawing it, such as a shader that fails to compile, fails for good and names what was left out, though the engine exits successfully.

A worker uploads the finished video in parts of at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES, under Cloudflare's request limit, each with its SHA-256, and completes it with the SHA-256 of the whole file, at most SREDITOR_MAX_RENDER_BYTES. Parts go to disk as they arrive, never whole into memory; an upload left incomplete expires after 24 hours. Downloads are not split.

Render workers are GPU machines running the sreditor worker image (srstudio plus a pinned scene-render engine), registered by an instance admin. Each has its own worker token, pulls jobs over HTTPS and never needs an inbound port, reports its GPUs, engine version and srstudio commit, takes srstudio's GPU lock around every engine call and renders with scene-render encode --parallel auto. Splitting one video across machines waits for scene-render to split and join it.

An episode keeps reviews, each its own append-only record: reviewer (the user; for a token, the token too), when, optionally the media file reviewed with the time ranges seen, Markdown notes and a verdict (approved, changes_requested, rejected). Owners and editors add them; none is edited; only an owner or the reviewer deletes one. The episode shows its latest verdict; publishing warns, never blocks, when it is not approved or there is none.

Search finds words in one channel's writing with an FTS5 index that triggers keep current: episode titles, summaries, research, sources, screenplays, short scripts, pitches, library, third-party media and context, never waivers. A person's text is only words, never FTS5 syntax. Results name kind, id, episode or pitch, snippet and the call that opens them; they page by cursor and need channels:read.

An episode may have a vertical short script, stored and revised on its own: length, language, voice, then blocks in order, each from start_s to end_s with a function (hook, development, turn, punch, cta), voice-marked speech and an optional reaction (1-5), plus on-screen texts of at most 90 characters that work without sound and move with their blocks when measured times apply. Broken markup or times are refused; gaps, a hook past 3 s, no final punch or speech too long (by the recorded voice) only warn.

sreditor stays compatible with srstudio, Pedro's scene-render toolkit: owners and editors export an episode as a zip srstudio reads unchanged: the take timeline (timeline.json, takes in seconds with word timings), a WAV per take with its SHA-256, the bible (bible/cast.json, relationships.json) with the library entries the episode uses and any other complete ones, and the beats (assets/poses.json), written from a pinned copy of srstudio's vocabularies. Each missing piece is listed instead of a broken file.

A short-script block may carry beats, each at a time inside the block for one character of the cast: eyes, mouth, arms and wear from srstudio's closed toon vocabularies and an optional prop event. Beats are at least 0.15 s apart and the first starts at 0; a value outside the vocabulary is refused, and an episode whose style has no beats keeps them without exporting them.

A library character is a srstudio bible entry: world, status (canon or placeholder), kind (person, animal, object, archetype), the rig that draws it (such as toon-dog), look, who they are, comic role (straight, instigator, victim, chaos, know-it-all), what never changes, open questions and voice. Each canon fact cites a published episode of the channel, how it shows (line, drawn, voice, seen) and a quote. Places keep slug, world and description; the library records relationships between pairs of characters.
A channel's library also holds props: a name, slug, description and the srstudio registry name that draws it (such as laptop or papers). Beats refer to props by slug.

Episodes, characters, places, props and visual styles carry a slug in srstudio's form (lowercase words joined by hyphens), unique within the channel, proposed from the name and editable until the first export; an episode also keeps an integer seed, so a rebuild in srstudio draws the same frames.

A voice belongs to a character, not to a script: an ElevenLabs premade voice id and name with stability, similarity boost and style (0 to 1) and speed (0.7 to 1.2). Each short-script block names who speaks, a character of the channel's library or the episode's narrator voice, and its voice markup tags use srstudio's audio-tag names, so an export turns them into srstudio's direction fields (tags, emphasis, pauses) with the line text clean.

Long texts people and agents write (research notes, pitch notes and summaries, context answers, editorial guidelines) are Markdown. Pages and PDF books show them formatted through one renderer: headings, emphasis, lists, quotes, code and http, https or mailto links, never raw HTML or images. Where a summary is cut short it shows as plain text. JSON and MCP keep the text as written, Excel cells stay plain text, and MCP tool descriptions say which fields take Markdown.

A library visual style has a name, slug, look description, srstudio style (cutout, ink, soft, cel, stick, toon, collage, saga or gloss, which fixes frame size and fps) and, as data: palette (#RRGGBB by role), fonts by role, cut rhythm (shortest and average shot in seconds), smallest text in px at frame height and safe zone (% per edge). The srstudio export carries them in style.json. Each episode picks at most one style of its channel; removing it leaves those episodes without one.

Owners and editors can generate an episode's voice-over from its short script with ElevenLabs; the key lives only in SREDITOR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, and without it the feature is hidden. Each block is its own take in its speaker's voice, with word timings; the same text, voice, settings, model and language reuses the earlier take and spends no credits. Takes join into a voice_over media file ending in a short fade and silence; measured block starts can replace planned times. Tests never call ElevenLabs.

Speech carries voice direction inline: [tag] or [tag:value] at a point, [tag]...[/tag] over a span, from one vocabulary defined once in voice_markup.py with each tag's ElevenLabs rendering per model (v2: <break> up to 3 s; v3: audio tags). A pause lasts what it says in both: v3 cannot time one, so the missing silence goes into the take between the words around it. Camera, sound and edit cues stay in the script for editing and are never spoken. Unknown tags, wrong values and unclosed spans are refused.

Before generating a voice-over, a person or agent can see its cost: per block the characters to speak and whether a stored take is reused, then the total characters and credits for the model. Each take returns its words with start and end in seconds through the API and MCP, and keeps a license record: provider, voice id and name, model, the account's plan and when it was made. A channel's brand may name a default narrator voice, used when a script names none.

An episode's waivers are the signed releases behind it (image, voice or location rights): a PDF, JPEG or PNG file of at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES with who signed, when and what it covers. They hold personal data, so only owners and editors see or change them; a token reads them only with the waivers:read scope and changes them only with editorial:write as well. Their files always download, never display inline.

sreditor is a social media channel manager. Its HTTP API manages channels, their accounts on each social platform, their brand kits and their Editorial guidelines, kept as statements in a [stmt](stmt-1.0.0.tar.gz) store. The same store is the single source of truth for this project's documents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and README.md), which sreditor generates.

## Install

You need Python 3.12+, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Node.js 24.12+ (for stmt).

```sh
tar -xzf stmt-1.0.0.tar.gz -C ~/.local/opt
export STMT_BIN=~/.local/opt/stmt-1.0.0/bin/stmt
uv sync
```

## Usage

```sh
uv run sreditor rules load        # after a checkout: load store/rules.csv into store/rules.sqlite
uv run sreditor render            # regenerate every document, store/rules.csv included, from the store
uv run sreditor render --check    # exit 1 if a document is out of date (for CI)
uv run sreditor serve --port 8000 # the public site at /, the API docs at /docs
```

## Tests

```sh
uv run pytest                       # unit tests, with coverage
uv run playwright install chromium  # once
uv run pytest e2e --no-cov          # public flows in Chromium, against Docker
```

## Design system

Raw values live only as tokens in `src/sreditor/web/static/tokens.css`; components are the Jinja macros in `src/sreditor/web/templates/_ui.html`. With `SREDITOR_DEV_PAGES=true`, /design shows every component in each state and theme; otherwise it answers 404.

## Configuration

Store settings come from flags, then environment variables (`STMT_BIN`, `STMT_DB`, `STMT_DOMAIN`, `STMT_SCOPE`), then `[tool.sreditor]` in `pyproject.toml`. Set `SREDITOR_PUBLIC_URL` to the exact origin people browse to: email links point there, and forms posted from any other origin are rejected. Set `SREDITOR_COOKIE_SECURE=false` only for local HTTP.

Emails go out through SMTP2GO when `SREDITOR_SMTP2GO_API_KEY` is set, from `SREDITOR_MAIL_SENDER` (for example `sreditor <noreply@your-domain>`), a sender verified in SMTP2GO; `SREDITOR_SMTP2GO_URL` picks a regional endpoint. They are sent beside each request and a failure is logged. Without a key, emails only go to the log, with tokens redacted unless `SREDITOR_MAIL_LOG_TOKENS=true` (development only).

## Docker

Copy `.env.example` to `.env`, set the user that owns `./var`, then run `docker compose up --build`. The API listens on 127.0.0.1:8000. The container keeps its stmt store in the data volume (`./var/rules.sqlite`) and loads the project's rules from `store/rules.csv` each time it starts.

To reach it over the internet, create a Cloudflare Tunnel, route its public hostname to `http://sreditor:8000`, and set `CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN`, `COMPOSE_PROFILES=tunnel` and `SREDITOR_PUBLIC_URL=https://<that hostname>` in `.env`; no port is opened. Rate limits count each visitor by `SREDITOR_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` (`CF-Connecting-IP` in Docker), which Cloudflare sets, not by X-Forwarded-For, whose first entry the visitor writes.

`sreditor doctor` checks `.env`, the store owner, the rules store, the public URL, email, the tunnel and whether the app answers; `--fix` writes `.env`. `--environment development|production` and `--hostname` are remembered there. With `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` exported in the shell (Tunnel Edit, DNS Edit), it creates or updates the tunnel `sreditor-<environment>` and its DNS record. Production needs an https hostname and SMTP2GO.

## Changing a rule or this README

Never edit a generated file. Run `uv run sreditor rules load`, revise the statement with `stmt create` or `stmt revise`, then run `uv run sreditor render` and commit `store/rules.csv` with the documents. Each statement's id is shown next to it.

The /terms and /privacy pages show the statements in the `terms` and `privacy` categories, ordered by id. Revise them in the store; the pages change on the next request.
